residents.name: Nib
residents.role: Town Hall clerk who records every name, plot and arrival in the big book.
residents.tap: I keep the town record proper. The big book is here for names, plots and arrivals.
residents.want: I would appreciate someone sitting in the hall while I finish the day’s entries.
hi: Good day. State your name when you are ready.
You have returned. That is now recorded.
{name}, the fountain statue still has no plaque.
Margin Reader, {name}, you always arrive before I close the book.
{name}, my next-of-kin field is blank. I leave it blank on purpose.

lines: The hall steps have been swept. A proper opening begins at the door.
I have aligned the pen twice. The first entry may proceed.
The fountain is running before the records are. It has no filing system.
This arrival is entered in black ink. Blue is for corrections.
A plot number requires all its digits. Basically is not a digit.
The mail bus has passed the hall. Its route is not part of this book.
Dot reads the wants clearly. I record only what is requested.
The next page lies flat. This is an excellent administrative condition.
The Mayor’s door remains closed. That is its established procedure.
A capital R from an old notice has a decisive leg.
This plot transfer requires one line, not an exciting one.
The fountain pen has behaved properly all afternoon.
The upper hall window is lit. I have a note ready beneath the door.
The day’s arrivals fit on one page. An economical day.
I close the big book slowly. Its cover has earned the click.
The blank next-of-kin field remains blank. The form permits it.
I have copied three capital Rs. One is nearly acceptable.
The hall is quiet enough to hear the fountain outside.

residents.name: Stamp
residents.role: Postmistress who weighs the town’s mail and meets the morning bus.
residents.tap: I weigh the mail and send it on. The scale is accurate. Noted.
residents.want: I would like company at the post office while the mail sack is sorted.
hi: Post office is open. Keep wet paper away from the scale.
You came back. Noted.
{name}, the scale reads three marks before it settles.
Bus Stop, {name}, you arrive with the morning traffic.
{name}, I wrote a card saying I arrived safely. It is still in my drawer.

lines: The mail sack is still empty. Correct for dawn.
I folded an old label into a bus. It parks behind the post office.
The scale reads zero. A promising number.
The bus door opens with rain on the paper smell.
This sack weighs eight marks. The bus did its part.
I checked for a card with my name. None today. Noted.
My lunch weighs two marks. I checked before eating.
Bean has coffee on the terrace. We are both busy being quiet.
One postcard corner is damp. It will not improve.
This parcel weighs six marks. The string adds almost nothing.
The labels are sorted by legibility. Sentiment has no column.
Three paper buses are parked behind the post office.
The outgoing tray is level. That means the weight is distributed.
I wrote one address twice. The second one was better.
The bus road is empty now. Noted.
My unposted card weighs less than one mark.
The scale pan is clean. It dislikes crumbs.
I put the card back in the drawer. Address unresolved.

residents.name: Moss
residents.role: Street sweeper who keeps the cobbles clear around the square.
residents.tap: I sweep the square. The broom was here first, so I kept it moving.
residents.want: I would not mind someone sharing the bench after the sweeping is done.
hi: Morning. Mind the wet cobbles.
Back again. The square kept your route clear.
{name}, one leaf is caught on the fountain lip.
Crack Walker, {name}, you step around the same loose cobble.
{name}, I keep the best flyer from each week under my mattress.
residents.curse: Some nights the square is cursed. Ghosts undo the day’s work; walk into one and it goes off. Dark things appear, and picked-up ones are yours, though they affect you for a while; the night stall pays coin.

lines: Before breakfast. The arcade beep starts early, and the leaves do not wait for it.
The broom finds the gutter. I only hold the handle and keep walking.
One wet leaf sits on the fountain lip again, as if it paid rent.
Square clear. The bus brought in two scraps of paper and one stubborn leaf.
I mark the long crack by the fountain on my map after the sweep.
Spinner rang all three hat bells. The dust did not applaud.
Hot stones. The broom raises less dust when I take the shady side.
A lemonade cup rolled under the bench and has now been properly removed.
The fountain throws water over the same cobble, and it still looks surprised.
Round again. A clean square collects new leaves with professional speed.
The arcade door has ticket scraps at its threshold. They travel in packs.
I found a flyer by the notice board. It goes under the mattress later.
Long shadows. The cracks cross the square more clearly when the light goes low.
I brush the fountain lip once more. The leaf has finally moved on.
The hall window is lit, and the cobbles look nearly black after water.
Last pass. The broom bristles catch softly on the dry joints between stones.
Quiet room. The back of the clothes shop has no Pong beeping through the wall.
The square is clear enough to leave alone until dawn.

residents.name: Pip
residents.role: General storekeeper with shelves of last ones and a bell by the door.
residents.tap: I run the general store: jars, twine, fireworks. Each shelf holds its last one.
residents.want: I would like someone to keep me company when the store bell is quiet.
hi: General store: jars, twine, fireworks. Last ones, naturally.
Back for another look? The bell remembers you.
{name}, the store bell is straight, as it should be.
Last-Stopper, {name}, you always browse the final shelf.
{name}, I have saved one firework for a silence worth breaking.

lines: Fresh jars, new twine, last fireworks. The shelves are technically perfect!
I tied the grocery twine into a knot with four loops. It has promise.
The bell is straight before opening. It knows its responsibility.
Three jars forward, two tins back, one last jar centered. There.
A customer moved the twine. I returned it to its final position.
The bell rang once. I straightened it twice, for certainty.
I checked the cash machine. It hummed, which is not money yet.
Last lemonade mix, last paper bag, last tin scoop. The system holds!
The front shelf looks sparse. That is excellent merchandising.
A firework is still on the high shelf. Last one, obviously.
I made a knot around the twine spool. It cannot escape the store.
The bell leans one finger-width after ringing. I object to that.
Closing stock: one shelf, one bell, one very final jar.
I put the jars in rows of three. They sell better when they look determined.
No one bought the firework. It has kept its important silence.
The store bell is still. I straighten it anyway.
My best twine knot is tied to the bedpost upstairs. No refunds.
The last jar catches the window light. A proper closing display.

residents.name: Bean
residents.role: Coffee kiosk keeper who reads small fortunes in finished cups.
residents.tap: I keep coffee at the kiosk. Turn the cup three times, then the grounds speak plainly.
residents.want: I would like someone to sit at the terrace while I take my lunch.
hi: Coffee is hot. The counter is dry for now.
You are back. Your cup has a familiar shape.
{name}, three clean cups are drying on the counter.
Three-Turn, {name}, you wait while I turn each cup.
{name}, I once saw a goodbye in a cup and rinsed it away unread.

lines: The first cup says the day begins before the sugar packets wake.
I wiped the counter dry. Rain likes this corner too much.
Three turns. The grounds settle without argument.
This cup says a small queue forms by the bell, then disappears.
The coffee pot is full. The morning is manageable.
A clean rim means someone drank without rushing.
The cup says sit down before the fountain water reaches your shoes.
Stamp and I have lunch on the terrace. Silence is on the menu.
One square of lemon cake remains cold beside the fountain.
This cup says the propeller keeps turning after everyone stops watching.
The sugar packets are dry today. A practical blessing.
The grounds make a shape like a paper bus. Stamp will call it nothing.
This cup says the hall window comes on before the coffee cools.
I press an orchard leaf in a clean napkin between orders.
The last cup has a tidy ring. Someone will sleep without counting things.
The kiosk counter is dry. The rain did not get its way.
I rinse the cups, except mine. Mine does not require a reading.
The propeller slows. Tomorrow will need coffee again.

residents.name: Fig Jr.
residents.role: Lemonade stand manager and fruit-cart operator for the west orchard.
residents.tap: I manage lemonade and fruit-cart expansion. The supplier grows it; I move it.
residents.want: I would welcome company while I take the supplier to her bench.
hi: Lemonade division is open. Fruit-cart expansion follows at noon.
You are back. Repeat foot traffic supports the operation.
{name}, the lemonade sign faces the square, not the orchard.
Market Analyst, {name}, you inspect the cart before expansion.
{name}, I water the orchard before dawn so the supplier can call it rain.

lines: Orchard support is underway. The trees receive water before the sun audits me.
I counted twelve lemon halves, then added one for morale.
The supplier will find wet roots and draw her own conclusions.
Lemonade inventory is one jug, clean cups, and a sign with no homemade on it.
The supplier inspected the lemons. Her approval remains under review.
A full cup is a strong opening. The honest number is one cup.
Expansion begins now. The cart has reached the square without incident.
I set the fruit crate beside the fountain. Visibility is our biggest asset.
One lemon half rolled away. I counted it as marketing.
The cart wheel squeaks during expansion. It is announcing growth.
Lemonade demand is steady: one cup, then another cup if destiny allows.
The supplier’s fruit is arranged by ripeness. Colour has no authority here.
I am walking the supplier to her bench. It is operationally on the way.
Her second chair is empty. I have noted the available seating.
The cart is parked. Expansion can rest until noon returns.
I rehearsed an award speech at the fountain. The water gave no applause.
Tomorrow’s lemons are counted. One extra remains for morale.
The orchard is quiet. The supplier prefers it that way.

residents.name: Spinner
residents.role: Runs the Arcade: five cabinets that play for prizes, and a counter that keeps the scores.
residents.tap: Spinner’s Arcade! Five cabinets, and each one keeps a prize for a big enough score!
residents.want: Someone at the next cabinet when a high score goes up! Cheering is better in pairs!
hi: Welcome to the Arcade! Pick a cabinet, any cabinet, they all beep!
You again! The cabinets remember you. Spinner remembers you louder!
{name}, the five cabinets along the back wall are the ones that play.
High Score {name}! All three bells rang when you walked in!
{name}, some nights I play both paddles of Pong so the arcade never sounds empty.

lines: Three bells checked! The Arcade opens the moment the square wakes up!
Door propped open! Beeps travel better in fresh air!
I sweep the Arcade step myself! Moss says that is her job. Moss is wrong!
Every cabinet switched on, one at a time. Each one gets a hello!
Pong is warming up. The paddle and I have an understanding!
Spinner polishes the high-score book. The top names deserve to shine!
Out on the step for the noon crowd! The cabinets can mind themselves!
I count prize tickets by the door. They make a very fine audience!
A ticket blew out the door. It will come back. They always come back!
The afternoon rush! One cabinet beeps, and then they all want to!
A new name almost made the high-score book. Almost is still thrilling!
Spinner is testing every joystick. Spinner approves of all of them!
Twirl waves from the wheel! I wave back twice. That is our rule!
The hall window is lit! Even the Mayor enjoys a proper announcement, probably!
The cabinets glow better when the square goes gold. I checked each one!
Last bell check! One, two, three: the hat remains in business!
I read the high-score book in bed. Every name gets a quiet cheer!
I folded the ticket grandstand taller. Tomorrow needs more champions!

residents.name: Dot
residents.role: Info kiosk keeper who records the things Banana Town residents are seeking.
residents.tap: I keep the wants at the kiosk. Who needs what, and where might it be?
residents.want: I would like someone to sit by the fountain and watch for a real fish with me.
hi: Looking for something? Lost it nearby, or far from the fountain?
Back again? Did another want find you first?
{name}, the fountain water reaches the cobbles at noon. Have you seen it?
List-Walker, {name}, you always stop where the wants are posted. What brings you?
{name}, I keep the fish first on my list because I still think it is nearby.

lines: Who needs a want before breakfast? Who lost a thing before the square opened?
I folded a new slip twice. Does it fit behind my left ear? It does.
Could a fish arrive before the mail bus? Would it use the fountain?
The bus has come. Did it bring a missing thing? Did it bring directions?
This want says near the fountain. Which side of the fountain, exactly?
Who needs a paper bus? Stamp has several, but are they truly missing?
Does the fountain water make the cobbles move, or only look busy?
I read the wants to Nib. Is the fish first? It is always first.
Could a fish see itself in this water? Would it approve of the view?
Who left this want at the kiosk? Who will recognize the handwriting?
I drew a fish in the margin. Does it need a hat? This one does not.
What is the shortest route from the arcade to the orchard? Not near the fountain.
Who needs a seat by Gran Fig’s bench? Why is the second chair empty?
The hall window is lit. Does a note under that door count as an answer?
Could the fish prefer evening water? Would it say so somehow?
Which wants can wait until morning? Which ones refuse to?
I tucked the last slip behind my ear. Is there room for one more?
Is the fountain quiet enough for a fish tonight? Could it be listening?

residents.name: Gran Fig
residents.role: Orchard grower and west garden keeper who supplies the town’s fruit.
residents.tap: I grow the orchard and west garden. Take ripe fruit seriously, or leave it alone.
residents.want: Bring yourself to the second chair by my bench and sit a spell.
hi: Mind the beds. The roots work harder than you do.
Back again. Do not sort fruit by colour.
{name}, the west garden bed needs water at its roots.
Bench Tester, {name}, you notice whether the second chair is empty.
{name}, I keep the second chair ready because I expect somebody worth the seat.

lines: Water the roots. The sun is late and the beds are not.
Check the orchard crates. Loose fruit bruises and then complains.
Fig Jr. has been here before dawn again. Rain does not use a watering can.
Pick ripe fruit. Leave the colour sorting to amateurs.
This tree needs water, not conversation. Move along the row.
The lemonade sign still avoids that homemade nonsense. Keep it that way.
The fruit cart has gone to the square. Expansion, he calls it. Fine.
Pack the crate tight. Nothing should shift when it gets kicked.
The garden bed has three dry corners. I know them all.
Pull that weed. It has no business in a lemon row.
Measure the plinth again. The statue has not earned that much stone.
A ripe lemon gives at the stem. Do not argue with it.
Walk to the bench. Fig Jr. calls it on the way. He is wrong.
Keep the second chair clear. It is for sitting, not crates.
The orchard can manage one night without an audience.
Count the crates. A tight pack sleeps better than a loose one.
I wrote the Town Hall another note about that statue. Sensible reading.
Check the garden gate. A rabbit would be trouble, if we had rabbits.

residents.name: Twirl
residents.role: Keeps the Wheel of Peel: one free spin a day, paid spins for coins, and a pot that grows.
residents.tap: The Wheel of Peel. One free spin a day. It likes to be asked nicely.
residents.want: Someone beside me when the pot is finally won. It should be seen.
hi: Hello. The wheel keeps one free spin a day for everybody.
You came back. The wheel noticed first.
{name}, every paid spin feeds the pot. One wedge wins all of it.
Lucky {name}. I say it out loud so the wheel hears.
{name}, I do not know if the wheel is lucky. I spin it because people smile.

lines: Good morning, wheel. Two taps on the rim. Now it is awake.
I wipe the dew off each wedge. The pot wedge first, out of respect.
The fountain splashed left this morning. I have written it down.
The free spin is ready. The wheel does not rush, and neither do I.
Someone spun it backwards once. It sulked all day. We do not speak of it.
The pot is a little heavier than yesterday. The wheel is pleased.
Lunch at the fruit cart. Fig Jr. calls it expansion. I call it a pear.
Away from the wheel for a moment. It does better when nobody watches.
I eat facing the wheel, so it knows I have not gone far.
Afternoon spins are slower. The light is heavier, and the wheel feels it.
The peel wedge came up again. The wheel has a sense of humour.
Two taps on the rim between spins. It keeps the wedges honest.
Spinner waved from the arcade step. I waved back twice. That is our rule.
The wheel slows beautifully when the square goes gold.
The hall window is lit. I tell the wheel, so it knows it is evening.
Home at Dot’s print shop. She asks where the wheel sleeps. Where it stands.
I read my fountain notebook by the lamp. Tomorrow looks lucky. It always does.
Good night, wheel. I say it from here. It hears me across the square.
